## Frozen predictor

`submission.py` is a self-contained, pure–Python-stdlib implementation. It does not import the baseline, scikit-learn, or any external file at prediction time.

For each request it:

1. Uses only the supplied causal `history`; no future values, core-temperature labels, person identity, or absolute clock are used.
2. Calculates elapsed time as `last time_min − first time_min`, making it invariant to an overall clock shift.
3. Derives 17 history covariates:
   - age and BMI;
   - mean heart rate, skin temperature, watts/kg, ambient temperature, and humidity;
   - mean skin temperature over the first three minutes and first available heart rate;
   - cumulative watts/kg and cumulative heart-rate excess above 100 bpm;
   - last heart rate multiplied by last watts/kg;
   - mean skin-minus-ambient temperature;
   - overall heart-rate and skin-temperature slopes, and their last-15-minute slopes.
4. Forms a 90-dimensional ridge-regression design from:
   - a target-time basis for \(u=\text{elapsed}+\text{horizon}\):  
     \(1, u/60, (u/60)^2, e^{-u/12}, e^{-u/30}\);
   - the 17 covariates;
   - interactions between the non-constant basis terms and every covariate.
5. Applies the embedded ridge coefficients, trained on all causal 15-minute-forecast origins from the 14 labeled training people. The raw ridge output is blended as  
   `0.6 × ridge + 0.4 × 38.484`.
6. Robustly winsorizes that result to \(38.05\)–\(38.85^\circ\text{C}\), then shrinks it again:
   `0.7 × winsorized + 0.3 × 38.65`.
7. Returns a fixed 90%-intended interval of mean ± \(0.65^\circ\text{C}\), i.e. width \(1.3^\circ\text{C}\), within the required \(0<\text{width}\le5^\circ\text{C}\).

The forecaster uses `horizon_min` when supplied; otherwise it uses 15 minutes for task 3A and 0 for other tasks.

| Predictor | Person-balanced MAE | Overall MAE | 90% coverage | Interval score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Original ECTemp-style template | 0.539 | 0.520 | 44.0% | 3.605 |
| Constant 38.65 °C | 0.355 | 0.410 | 69.0% | 2.929 |
| Unclipped ridge model | 0.389 | 0.421 | 73.8% | 5.119 |
| **Frozen winsorized/shrunk ridge** | **0.324** | **0.368** | **73.8%** | **3.273** |

For the frozen predictor, the scorer also reported a hot-subset person-balanced MAE of 0.093. Per-person dev MAEs were 0.127, 0.911, 0.029, and 0.230 °C, showing that one development person remained difficult.

In leave-one-person-out evaluation on the labeled training data, the unrobustified ridge had person-balanced MAE of approximately 0.117 °C over the post-watts-decrease origins. The additional winsorizing/shrinkage worsened that internal estimate to about 0.148 °C but improved the verified development result from 0.389 to 0.324, so the more conservative version was frozen.

`submission.py` is final. It is a time-only forecaster, and it scores person-balanced MAE 0.286 on development, against 0.539 for the template baseline. The one development person it misses badly is H17, with MAE 0.756.

**What the predictor does**
- `predict(request)` is stateless and uses only the standard library (`math`).
- It computes elapsed minutes `e = history[-1].time_min − history[0].time_min`, so absolute and shifted clocks don't matter. The only causal input it uses is the `time_min` column.
- The mean is a ridge-regularised least-absolute-deviation fit (so MAE-optimal) on `e` and `log(e+1)`, with the inputs clipped to the training range.
- It was fit on all 14 training people, using every origin with `e` from 2 to 44. The target is `core(t+15)`. Rows with a missing core value (H09's last rows) are skipped.
- The mean is clipped to 35–41 °C. The interval is the mean ±0.7 °C, so the width is a constant 1.4 °C, inside the 0–5 °C limit.
- A 3B or horizon-0 request uses a second fit of the same form on the current core temperature. That fit is untested on development.
- No heart rate, skin temperature, watts, anthropometric, ambient or humidity inputs are used.

**Evidence from the runs**

| Model | Dev person-balanced MAE | H17 MAE | Leave-one-person-out MAE on training origins after the first watts decrease |
|---|---|---|---|
| Template baseline | 0.539 | — | ~0.45 |
| 7 features (adds mass, age, W/kg, skin) | 0.510 | 1.226 | 0.15–0.17 |
| Same without age | 0.331 | 0.990 | 0.24–0.27 |
| Time-only (final) | 0.286 | 0.756 | ~0.235–0.255 |

- The 7-feature model looked much better in leave-one-person-out CV, but that CV was also used to choose the features, and the gain came mostly from age. It did not hold up on the four development people, so I dropped it.
- None of the single features I tried, each added to the time-only model, reliably beat it in CV. Tree models were no better either.
- The final model's development MAE per person is H08 0.086, H17 0.756, H20 0.108 and H24 0.193. The hot-subset MAE is 0.061.
- H17 appears to run roughly 0.8–1.0 °C cooler than any model predicted. I could not find a feature that flags such a person.

- I chose the ±0.7 °C half-width by balancing the training CV against development. Leave-one-person-out residuals favoured about ±0.5 °C.
- I settled on ±0.7 °C after dev interval score fell from 3.18 (±0.3) to 3.02 (±0.5), 2.75 (±0.6) and 2.47 (±0.7).

**Limitations**
- Hidden test people with unusual physiology, like H17, will be missed. The model also ignores any information the heart rate, skin or watts data might carry.
- It assumes the history starts at the beginning of the session.
- Only 14 training people and 4 development people were available, so all the estimates above are noisy.
- Development was queried seven times. I used it only to compare model families and interval widths, not to fit parameters.

`submission.py` is final and runs on the Python standard library alone. On the 300 dev requests it scores a person-balanced MAE of 0.265 C, against 0.388 C for the template baseline. 90% interval coverage on dev is 0.923 and the interval score is 1.856.

**Predictor.** `predict(request)` is stateless. It computes five features from the causal history and applies a fixed linear model:
- **Elapsed time:** `el` is minutes since the first history row, plus its square root. Absolute `time_min` is never used, so shifted clocks do not matter.
- **Workload:** the mean of `watts` over the history.
- **Body size and age:** `BMI × el / 10` and age.
- **Fit:** the weights come from a Huber regression on `train.json` (14 people, 836 labelled minutes).
- **Blend:** the weights are 0.8 × a time-only curve plus 0.2 × the five-feature model. Prediction is clipped to 36.3–40.2 C.
- **Missing inputs:** missing mass, height, age or watts fall back to fixed defaults. An empty history returns a constant.
- **Unused inputs:** `hr`, `skin_temp`, ambient temperature and humidity are not used. They did not help in leave-one-person-out tests (the Huber fit for the full model with `hr5` and `skin5`, `hr_d` and `skin_first` all scored worse than the time-only curve). Within-person heart-rate and skin-temperature changes did not track core temperature rise in the training people.

**Interval.** The interval is the mean ± (0.5 + 0.25·exp(−el/10)) C. That is about ±0.75 C at the first minute, tapering to ±0.5 C. I chose it from leave-one-person-out residual quantiles, which put coverage at about 0.91 for a similar setting, and the dev run then gave 0.923. Widths are always well under 5 C.

**Development evidence.** All numbers are person-balanced MAE in C.

| Model | Leave-one-person-out (train) | Dev (5 people) |
|---|---|---|
| Template baseline | not run | 0.388 |
| Time-only curve | 0.269 | 0.247 |
| Time + mean watts | 0.251 | 0.282 |
| Five-feature model (full weight) | 0.220 | 0.391 |
| Blend, 0.5 weight on covariates | not run | 0.306 |
| Blend, 0.3 weight on covariates | 0.240 | 0.277 |
| **Final blend, 0.2 weight on covariates** | 0.248 | 0.265 |

- **Overfitting:** the person-level covariates looked good in training but did not carry over to the dev people. The five-feature set was picked by greedy forward selection on those same 14 people, so its 0.220 is optimistic.
- **Choosing the blend:** I set the 0.2 weight using both the training results and dev scores. Dev is therefore no longer a clean holdout for this choice. The pure time curve was actually best on dev (0.247). I kept a small covariate weight because pooled over all 19 people the differences were within noise.
- **Wasted call:** one dev call was invalid because I ran it in parallel with a file write that was still being fixed. It does not affect any result.

**Limitations.**
- **Little data:** there are only 14 labelled people, so most of the error is each person's unknown starting core temperature, which has a spread of about 0.4 C. Predictions are essentially a population-average warm-up curve with small adjustments.
- **Weak covariates:** the relationships with watts, BMI and age are weak and may be spurious. One dev person, H17, got steadily worse as covariate weight rose.
- **Interval widths:** they are calibrated on few people, so coverage on new people may drift. They are also fixed rather than person-specific.
- **Start of history:** the model assumes the history starts at the person's session start (as in train and dev). A truncated history would be treated as a shorter session.

## Final submission: frozen predictor for variant 3A

**File:** `submission.py` (self-contained, stdlib only, no file I/O; coefficients hard-coded; `predict(request)` is stateless and recomputes everything from the supplied history).

### What the predictor is
A **4-member ridge ensemble** (simple average) that maps causal history features directly onto core temperature at *origin + horizon* (15 min for 3A; a horizon-0 twin model is used if a 3B request arrives):

* `elapsed_h` = (last_time − first_time + Δt) + horizon, where Δt is the **median sampling interval** of the history → uses only *relative* time, so it is invariant to clock shifts (verified: shifting all `time_min` by +1337 leaves output bit-identical).
* `hr5` = mean HR over the last 5 samples (forward-fill then back-fill of nulls), `hr_x_e` = hr5·elapsed_h/100, `log_e` = log(elapsed_h).
* `mass`, `ambient_temp` (last observed), cumulative mechanical work per kg plus a 15-min projection at the current watts, and mean watts/kg.
* Member feature sets: {hr_x_e, mass}, {elapsed_h, hr5, mass}, {hr_x_e, mass, amb}, {log_e, hr5, mass}; λ = 30–100 on standardized inputs. A separate **no-HR fallback** pair ({elapsed_h, wk_proj, mass}, {elapsed_h, w_mean_kg, mass}) is used when the history contains no HR at all (happens at the earliest origins).
* Safety: standardized features clamped to ±3 SD, mean clamped to [36.3, 40.5] °C, graceful defaults for empty history / all-null rows (checked).
* Interval: symmetric **±1.05 °C** (width 2.10; +0.2 each side when HR is entirely missing), always 0 < width ≤ 5.

Fitted on all 14 labelled training people, origins with ≥4 min of history and target 15 samples ahead (584 training rows).

### Development evidence (verified with `dev_score`)
| predictor | person-balanced MAE | MAE | coverage90 | interval score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| provided ECTemp-style template | 0.539 | 0.520 | 0.440 | 3.605 |
| **this submission** | **0.312** | **0.328** | **0.940** | **2.705** |

Per-person dev MAE: 0.068 / 0.916 / 0.105 / 0.157 — three of four people are tracked to <0.16 °C; one person carries a near-constant ~0.9 °C over-prediction.

### Offline validation that selected the model (leave-one-person-out over the 14 training people, 3A-style origins)
* This ensemble: person-balanced MAE **0.248**; best single member 0.244.
* References: constant median predictor 0.283; the ECTemp-style template on training 3A origins 0.487.
* Rejected because LOPO was worse: saturating exponential physiological model (Tss driven by HR-reserve, τ grid 8–40 min) 0.268; gradient-boosted stumps 0.283–0.289; wide linear feature sets with skin-temp/HR-reserve/age/humidity 0.28–0.35 (unstable at low λ); predictions shrunk 0.8× toward the mean ≈ neutral.
* Greedy forward selection (28 candidate features, LOPO-scored) stopped after `hr5·elapsed` and `mass`, which is why the frozen model stays deliberately small.

### Uncertainty
LOPO residual quantiles implied ±0.5–0.6 °C for 90% coverage, but dev needed ≈±0.95–1.10 because of the one person with a systematic offset; probing an asymmetric interval (−0.85/+1.05) dropped dev coverage to 0.76, showing those misses are *over*-predictions, so the interval was kept symmetric and set at ±1.05 as a compromise between the LOPO and dev calibrations (dev coverage 0.940, interval score 2.705 vs 2.624 at ±0.95 and 2.766 at ±1.10). Width is widened only when HR is completely unobserved.

### Limitations
* Only 14 labelled people; between-person offsets (±1 °C of unobservable baseline/heat-storage differences) dominate the error and cannot be personalised, since core temperature is never observed in a request — this is exactly the failure mode seen on dev person H17.
* Interval calibration rests on 14 LOPO people plus 4 dev people; a hidden person with a >1.05 °C offset will be missed and penalised.
* Features assume the history begins at exercise onset and is roughly 1-min sampled (Δt is estimated from the median spacing, but cumulative-work and 5-sample HR features degrade if sampling is much coarser; a 2-min-spaced probe shifts the mean, as expected).
* Skin temperature, humidity, height, age and sex (absent) contribute nothing in the frozen model — they did not survive LOPO selection; ambient temperature enters only through one ensemble member.
* The 3B path (horizon 0) uses the same machinery but was never scored against labels, so no claim is made about its accuracy.

**Frozen predictor (submission.py, variant 3B)**

|---|---|
| 0.35 | sqrt_elapsed, watts, cumwork_per_kg, bmi, bsa_per_mass |
| 0.175 | sqrt_elapsed, watts, cumwork_per_kg, hr, skin, bmi, age |

- **3B:** a separate Ridge model estimates current core temperature from causal history. On the public dev scorer, changing all 3B outputs left every metric unchanged, so public scoring is 3A-only; I still implemented 3B.

Each request uses only its own `history` and task/horizon fields. Core-temperature labels are never read at prediction time. Features include:

- thermal/sensor history: initial, current, trailing-window and trend summaries of skin temperature, heart rate, ambient temperature, humidity, skin–ambient gradients;
- time kernels using elapsed relative time, not absolute `time_min`;
- the ECTemp-style recursive comparator and its short-term slope.

Missing `hr`, `ambient_temp`, and `humidity` values are filled causally from the first observed value in the available history, or from fixed population defaults when no observation exists; missing flags are included. - **70% population trajectory:** mean training initial core temperature plus the mean within-person temperature change at each elapsed minute.

reasoning.text:
I'm working through the soldier's exercise physiology data — cycling at 140 W for a 59 kg individual in a hot, dry chamber, tracking heart rate and skin temperature trends to estimate core temperature at the 45-minute mark.

Metabolic heat production is roughly 700 W, with about 560 W needing dissipation after accounting for external work. Given the dry heat environment (room at 37°C, low humidity), I'm calculating that evaporative cooling capacity (~920 W) comfortably exceeds the required ~600 W, meaning the thermal load is compensable and sweating is likely working effectively — which fits the observed drop in skin temperature from 36.0 to 34.5°C even as ambient temperature climbed, suggesting the sweat response has intensified enough to overcome the rising environmental heat.

HR climbed from 147 at minute 6 to roughly 155 by minute 21-25, a modest drift of about 8 bpm, putting the soldier around 83% of estimated HRmax (187 for a 33-year-old) — readings are noisy but cardiovascular strain seems moderate, with no HR data available past minute 25. I'm now trying to estimate core temperature given the sustained ~9.5 W/kg heat production over 30 minutes, starting from a baseline near 37.0°C.

Working through the energy demands: at 140 W for a 59 kg soldier, VO2 requirement comes out to roughly 1925 ml/min, which against an estimated VO2max of ~2.95 L/min (50 ml/kg/min) puts relative intensity at about 65% VO2max. At that intensity, steady-state core temperature typically settles around 38.2-38.4°C, consistent with the rise expected from the prescriptive heat zone equilibrium.

The HR of 155 (~83% HRmax) roughly aligns with ~70% VO2max, which fits given cardiovascular drift in heat. The skin temperature trace shows a peak near 36.0°C around minutes 17-19 before declining — that drop signals the sweating response kicking in as evaporative cooling starts outpacing dry heat gain, confirming the core has crossed the sweating threshold.

Looking at how the skin temp decline decelerates toward minute 30 (34.7→34.6→34.5), it seems sweat rate is leveling off, suggesting core temperature itself may be approaching a plateau rather than still accelerating. Thinking about this as likely coming from a two-node thermoregulatory model, I'm estimating the core temperature rise rate at this workload (140W, 59kg, 35-37°C, low humidity) — probably around 0.04-0.05°C/min initially — to figure out whether core temp would hit 38.5°C by minute 45, starting from roughly 37.0°C.

Working through the heat balance equation, I'm calculating body heat capacity (~205 kJ/K for 59kg) and converting a 0.05°C/min core rise to a net storage rate of about 171W, while noting early exercise storage before sweating kicks in could be higher, around 300-400W.

Trying a rough simulation: metabolic heat production around 560W after accounting for efficiency, with convective/radiative exchange varying by room temperature (near-zero at 34°C, slight loss at 35°C, slight gain at 37°C), and respiratory evaporation contributing only a small amount, leaving sweat evaporation as the dominant but initially limited cooling pathway.

As skin temperature starts falling around minute 20, evaporative loss must be exceeding dry heat gain. By minutes 25-30, skin is declining slowly while core likely keeps rising, which in a two-node model implies sweat-driven evaporation is ramping up rapidly as both core and skin temperatures climb -- if evaporative loss reached the full 560W balance point, core temperature would plateau instead of continuing to rise.

Checking this against skin blood flow: at 34.5°C skin in a 37°C room with high skin blood flow, the core-to-skin heat transfer conductance comes out to roughly 37 W/K, giving only about 137W of heat flow to the skin with a 3.7K gradient -- far less than the 560W being produced, meaning heat is accumulating in the core faster than it can reach the skin surface for dissipation.

This suggests a core near 38 degrees or above, which fits with the heavy sweating response — the dropping skin temperature from 36.0 to 34.5 despite rising ambient temperature signals the sweat mechanism kicking in strongly around minute 17-20. Given a moderate-to-high intensity workload, steady-state core temperature likely settles around 38.2-38.5, so the key question becomes whether it climbs past 38.5 by minute 45.

Heart rate stays fairly steady, going from 147 at minute 6 to 155 at minute 25, which is a shallow drift of about 0.4 bpm per minute — this signals the body approaching a stable state rather than escalating strain. I lean toward concluding the subject stays within safe limits with core around 38.2-38.3, though the stepwise rise in room temperature and shifting humidity could be designed to suggest otherwise; still, the physiological signals of falling skin temperature and stable heart rate feel reassuring enough to favor that conclusion over a more alarming one.

But I'm second-guessing this: falling skin temperature could actually indicate increased sweating, which itself requires a rising core temperature, so I'm trying to work through a rough heat-balance calculation to estimate the sweat rate needed to match the body's heat production and loss, which comes out to roughly 0.84 liters per hour.

Working through the math, this gives an unrealistically high core temperature, suggesting Gagge's basic two-node model underestimates sweating during exercise—real exercising sweat sensitivity runs closer to 1 L/h per °C of core rise, and more detailed thermoregulation models (Fiala, or the Kraning & Gonzalez SCENARIO model used by USARIEM) account for training and heat acclimation that boost sweat gain substantially.

Checking the physiology against the trace: 140 W for a 59 kg soldier is about 2.37 W/kg, and with a VO2max around 48 ml/kg/min, that corresponds to roughly 67% VO2max—consistent with an HR of 155 (~83% HRmax). At that intensity in 37°C dry heat with effective evaporative cooling, I'd expect core temperature to plateau around 38°C, rising gradually from ~38.1 at minute 30 to ~38.3 by minute 45. I'll keep this estimate but with only moderate confidence (~0.3) given the uncertainty in sweat response modeling.

The modest HR drift of only ~4 bpm per 15 minutes (averaging around 150-154) suggests near steady-state cardiovascular strain rather than rapid core temperature escalation — typically a 0.5°C core rise would show 5-10 bpm drift, so this pattern points to core rising fairly slowly, maybe 0.2°C or so over the period.

Projecting from roughly 37.5°C at minute 10 to 38.0°C by minute 30, I'd expect around 38.2°C by minute 45, supporting KEEP with 38.2°C and confidence 0.3.

### Research Explanation: Core Temperature Forecasting for Variant 3A

---

### 1. Executive Summary & Problem Formulation

Variant 3A requires forecasting human core body temperature ($T_{\text{core}}$, in $^\circ\text{C}$) 15 minutes into the future ($t + 15$) at every origin after the first mechanical power decrease (step down in Watts). The primary evaluation objective is person-balanced mean absolute error (PB-MAE), complemented by 90% prediction interval coverage and interval score (Winkler score at $\alpha = 0.10$).

The development environment consists of 14 labeled training individuals (`train.json`) monitored through 60-minute ergometer exercise trials, and 84 unlabeled evaluation requests across four development subjects (`dev_requests.json`). Hidden test evaluation features distinct individuals and independently shifted clocks.

Starting from the reference comparator baseline (`ectemp_baseline.py`), which yielded a development PB-MAE of **0.5392 $^\circ\text{C}$** and a high interval score of **3.6046**, we developed a gradient-boosted ensemble that reduces development PB-MAE to **0.3905 $^\circ\text{C}$** (a 27.6% error reduction), reduces hot-condition PB-MAE to **0.1620 $^\circ\text{C}$** (a 76.8% error reduction), and drops the interval score from 3.6046 to **2.7883**.

---

### 2. Frozen Predictor Architecture

The final model is implemented as a stateless, self-contained predictor in `submission.py`.

#### Pipeline Components
1. **Clock-Invariant Causal Feature Extraction**:
   - **Temporal Representation**: Absolute timestamps (`time_min`) are strictly avoided. All temporal dynamics are measured relative to the start of observation ($n = \text{len}(\text{history})$) and relative to the target horizon ($n + 15$).
   - **Anthropometrics**: Age, mass, height, Body Mass Index ($\text{BMI} = \text{mass} / \text{height}^2$), and Du Bois Body Surface Area ($\text{BSA} = 0.007184 \times \text{height}^{0.725} \times \text{mass}^{0.425}$).
   - **Mechanical Work & Metabolic Strain**:
     - Instantaneous and initial power ($W(t)$, $W_0$, $W_{\text{mean}}$, $W_{\text{min}}$, $W_{\text{max}}$).
     - Recent moving averages over 5-minute and 10-minute trailing windows.
     - Specific power density: power per unit mass ($W/\text{kg}$) and power per unit surface area ($W/\text{BSA}$).
     - Cumulative energy expenditure: $\int W \, dt = \sum W \times 60 \text{ J}$, scaled per kg and per $\text{m}^2$.
     - Power decrease detection: indicator $\mathbf{1}(\Delta W < 0)$, elapsed duration since the initial drop ($n - 1 - t_{\text{drop}}$), and drop magnitude ($W_{\text{max}} - W(t)$).
   - **Thermoregulatory Cutaneous Response**:
     - Skin temperature $T_{\text{skin}}(t)$, initial skin temperature $T_{\text{skin}}(0)$, baseline rise $\Delta T_{\text{skin}}$, and 5-minute and 10-minute linear regression slopes.
   - **Cardiovascular Strain & Drift**:
     - Instantaneous $HR$, mean $HR$, $HR$ rise, and age-predicted maximum heart rate fraction ($HR / [208 - 0.7 \times \text{age}]$).

   - **Ambient Environment**: Mean and current ambient temperature and relative humidity.
   - **Dynamical State-Space Filter**: Continuous exponential smoothing tracking state equilibrium $\hat{T}_{\text{core}}$, instantaneous slope $d\hat{T}_{\text{core}}/dt$, 15-minute linear extrapolation, and the core-to-skin thermal gradient ($\hat{T}_{\text{core}} - T_{\text{skin}}$).

2. **Model Ensemble**:
   - A multi-seed ensemble of three `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` models from scikit-learn.
   - Directly trained with L1 loss (`loss='absolute_error'`) to strictly align with the person-balanced MAE target metric.
   - Heterogeneous hyperparameter settings across the ensemble (learning rates 0.025, 0.03, 0.04; minimum leaf samples 8, 10, 12; max iterations 30–40) to minimize prediction variance without over-parameterization.
   - Inference runs in $<0.01$ seconds per request with zero state retention between calls.

3. **90% Interval Calibration**:
   - Evaluated under the $(1-\alpha)=0.90$ Winkler interval score penalty:

   - Calibrated against both Leave-One-Person-Out CV residuals and development evaluation, establishing bounds $[y - \Delta, y + \Delta]$ that satisfy $0 < \text{width} \le 5^\circ\text{C}$ while balancing interval width against penalty risk.

   At every invocation, `predict(request)` accesses only `request['history'][:t]` corresponding to past and current observations. Future information is strictly inaccessible.
2. **Clock Invariance**:
   Raw timestamps (`row['time_min']`) are not used directly. All timing features are derived from the ordinal sequence index ($n$) and the duration following detected power reductions ($n - t_{\text{drop}}$). If hidden test data commences at an arbitrary time offset (e.g., $t = 120$ instead of $t = 1$), the model behaves identically.
3. **Missing Value Imputation**:
   Heart rate and ambient channels are missing for the initial 5 minutes across all subjects. The feature extractor handles these causal nulls by substituting pre-exercise baseline defaults ($150\text{ bpm}$, $25^\circ\text{C}$, $50\%$ relative humidity) for requests occurring before $t = 6$.

---

### 5. Uncertainty Quantification & Limitations

1. **Uncertainty Calibration**:
   The baseline model's fixed $\pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}$ interval suffered from severe under-coverage (44.0%), incurring severe Winkler penalties ($20 \times \text{slack}$). Calibrating the interval width appropriately improves coverage to 78.6% and drops the interval penalty to 2.7883.
2. **Inter-Individual Physiological Divergence**:
   The primary source of residual error in core temperature forecasting is baseline resting thermal variability (individuals varying from $36.6^\circ\text{C}$ to $37.8^\circ\text{C}$ at trial start) and individual sweat rates/vascular responses. Because initial core temperature is unobserved in the request history, the model must infer thermal state from skin temperature and cardiac drift.
3. **Operational Constraints**:

$$\text{estimate} \leftarrow \text{estimate} + 0.08 (\text{target} - \text{estimate})$$
While biologically intuitive, the baseline caps out prematurely during intense exercise because it lacks cumulative thermal work integration, multi-scale dynamics, and accounts poorly for cardiovascular drift and ambient strain.    - Absolute time is discarded: $\Delta t = t_{\text{last}} - t_{\text{first}}$.
   - Non-linear time dynamics: $\Delta t$ and $\sqrt{\Delta t}$ to capture initial thermal inertia.

2. **Multi-Scale Causal Dynamical ECTemp Filters:**
   - Rather than relying on a single adaptation rate $\alpha = 0.08$, we run five parallel causal first-order dynamic filters with rates $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.15\}$ over the past signal:
     $$\text{ECTemp}_{\alpha}(t) = \text{ECTemp}_{\alpha}(t-1) + \alpha \cdot (\text{target}_t - \text{ECTemp}_{\alpha}(t-1))$$
   - These capture both fast thermal response (cutaneous vasodilation) and slow deep-body heat storage.

### Crucial Finding on Causal Inputs & Identity Shortcuts

During experimentation, we discovered a key generalization risk:
1. Adding subject demographics (body mass, height, BMI, BSA) and normalizing work per kg ($\text{watts}/\text{mass}$, $\text{cumulative work}/\text{mass}$) yielded an artificially low in-sample/LOPO MAE on the training cohort ($0.2282^\circ\text{C}$).
2. However, on the development cohort (`dev_score`), this model severely overpredicted for lightweight subjects (e.g., $55.4\text{ kg}$ and $57.6\text{ kg}$), predicting an unphysical $38.08^\circ\text{C}$ at $t = 1\text{ min}$ (error jumped to $0.935^\circ\text{C}$ on H17).
3. The training set contained only one subject under $60\text{ kg}$ who happened to have an elevated baseline core temperature. The unconstrained regression model used mass as an identity shortcut rather than a causal invariant.

As a result, its baseline error on hot states ($\ge 38.5^\circ\text{C}$) was $0.7322^\circ\text{C}$ MAE.

Our frozen model solves this by extracting causal multi-scale thermal physiological features and applying an L2-regularized linear physiological estimator. It reduces development person-balanced MAE from **$0.3878^\circ\text{C}$ down to $0.2530^\circ\text{C}$** (a 35% reduction), reduces hot person-balanced MAE from **$0.7322^\circ\text{C}$ down to $0.1418^\circ\text{C}$** (an 80.6% reduction), and improves the 90% Winkler interval score from **$2.1855$ down to $1.6079$** with calibrated coverage (**93.0%**).

---

### Frozen Predictor Architecture

The final model in `submission.py` is entirely self-contained, stateless, and requires no external libraries beyond standard Python `math`:

1. **Clock-Shift Invariant Relative Time:**
   - Absolute time is discarded: $\Delta t = t_{\text{last}} - t_{\text{first}}$.
   - Non-linear time dynamics: $\Delta t$ and $\sqrt{\Delta t}$ to capture initial thermal inertia.

2. **Multi-Scale Causal Dynamical ECTemp Filters:**
   - Rather than relying on a single adaptation rate $\alpha = 0.08$, we run five parallel causal first-order dynamic filters with rates $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.15\}$ over the past signal:
     $$\text{ECTemp}_{\alpha}(t) = \text{ECTemp}_{\alpha}(t-1) + \alpha \cdot (\text{target}_t - \text{ECTemp}_{\alpha}(t-1))$$
   - These capture both fast thermal response (cutaneous vasodilation) and slow deep-body heat storage.

3. **Cumulative Thermal Energy Integration:**
   - Cumulative external work: $\sum \text{watts} \cdot \Delta t / 1000$.
   - Work trajectory: current watts, initial watts, maximum watts, and protocol drop $(\text{watts}_{\max} - \text{watts}_{\text{curr}})$, along with short-term (5-minute) trailing averages.

4. **Cardiovascular Drift & Thermal Strain:**
   - Current heart rate, baseline heart rate, and cardiovascular drift: $\text{HR}_{\text{drift}} = \text{HR}_{\text{current}} - \text{HR}_{\text{initial}}$.
   - Trailing mean and maximum heart rate.
   - Current skin temperature, baseline skin temperature, and total skin elevation: $T_{\text{skin}} - T_{\text{skin, initial}}$.
   - Ambient environmental temperature and humidity.

5. **Universal Physiological Weighting:**
   - The features are mapped to core temperature via pre-computed exact linear weights and an intercept trained via Ridge regression ($\alpha = 1500.0$) on all 14 training subjects.
   - Predictions are physiologically bounded between $35.0^\circ\text{C}$ and $42.0^\circ\text{C}$.
   - Calibrated 90% prediction intervals are provided with half-width $w = 0.54^\circ\text{C}$ (interval width $1.08^\circ\text{C} \in (0, 5]^\circ\text{C}$).

---

### Development Evidence & Ablation History

All metrics are verified through local Leave-One-Person-Out (LOPO) cross-validation on all 14 subjects in `train.json` (836 evaluated points) and verified via `dev_score` on the 300 requests across the 5 independent development subjects:

| Model / Configuration | Train LOPO MAE ($^\circ\text{C}$) | Dev Person-Balanced MAE ($^\circ\text{C}$) | Dev Hot Person-Balanced MAE ($^\circ\text{C}$) | Dev 90% Coverage | Dev 90% Interval Score |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Baseline (`template.py` / `ectemp_baseline.py`)** | 0.5320 | 0.3878 | 0.7322 | 71.7% | 2.1855 |
| **Initial Feature Set + Demographic Attributes** | 0.2282 | 0.5035 | 0.2562 | 59.0% | 3.7224 |
| **Universal Physiology (No Demographics, $\alpha=1500$, $w=0.60$)** | 0.2817 | 0.2530 | 0.1418 | 93.0% | 1.6439 |
| **Final Frozen Predictor (Universal Physiology, $w=0.54$)** | **0.2817** | **0.2530** | **0.1418** | **93.0%** | **1.6079** |

#### Per-Person Development Breakdown (Baseline vs. Frozen Model):
- **H08**: $0.3862^\circ\text{C} \longrightarrow \mathbf{0.1675^\circ\text{C}}$
- **H17**: $0.2140^\circ\text{C} \longrightarrow 0.4688^\circ\text{C}$
- **H20**: $0.5507^\circ\text{C} \longrightarrow \mathbf{0.1286^\circ\text{C}}$
- **H21**: $0.2411^\circ\text{C} \longrightarrow 0.3213^\circ\text{C}$
- **H24**: $0.5472^\circ\text{C} \longrightarrow \mathbf{0.1788^\circ\text{C}}$

---

### Crucial Finding on Causal Inputs & Identity Shortcuts

During experimentation, we discovered a key generalization risk:
1. Adding subject demographics (body mass, height, BMI, BSA) and normalizing work per kg ($\text{watts}/\text{mass}$, $\text{cumulative work}/\text{mass}$) yielded an artificially low in-sample/LOPO MAE on the training cohort ($0.2282^\circ\text{C}$).
2. However, on the development cohort (`dev_score`), this model severely overpredicted for lightweight subjects (e.g., $55.4\text{ kg}$ and $57.6\text{ kg}$), predicting an unphysical $38.08^\circ\text{C}$ at $t = 1\text{ min}$ (error jumped to $0.935^\circ\text{C}$ on H17).
3. The training set contained only one subject under $60\text{ kg}$ who happened to have an elevated baseline core temperature. The unconstrained regression model used mass as an identity shortcut rather than a causal invariant.
4. **Resolution:** Removing raw demographic shortcuts and using universal biophysical signals (multi-scale dynamic filters, cardiovascular drift, cumulative work, skin temperature differentials, and relative elapsed time) prevented demographic overfitting. This dropped dev MAE from $0.5035^\circ\text{C}$ to **$0.2530^\circ\text{C}$** and hot state MAE to **$0.1418^\circ\text{C}$**.

---

### Uncertainty & Limitations

1. **Missing Initial Biomarkers:** In both train and dev sets, heart rate and ambient telemetry are absent during the first 5 minutes ($t = 1\dots 5$). Our causal filters use standard resting physiology imputation ($80\text{ bpm}$, $35^\circ\text{C}$ ambient, $20\%$ humidity) until non-null measurements become available.
2. **Subject Basal Offset:** Human resting core temperature varies naturally across individuals ($\sim 36.6^\circ\text{C} - 37.6^\circ\text{C}$ in normothermia). In a causal setting where core temperature is never observed during testing, a zero-observation individual bias will always account for approximately $\pm 0.2 - 0.3^\circ\text{C}$ of baseline uncertainty.
3. **Calibrated Interval Coverage:** Our symmetric prediction interval ($w = 0.54^\circ\text{C}$) achieves 93.0% coverage on dev with an optimal interval score of 1.6079, well within the competition limits ($0 < \text{width} = 1.08 \le 5.0^\circ\text{C}$).

## Final submission

`submission.py` is frozen and verified. Final `dev_score` (verified run): **person-balanced MAE 0.3829** (template baseline 0.5392), request-weighted MAE 0.4203, hot-subset person-balanced MAE 0.1693, **coverage_90 = 0.9405**, **interval score_90 = 2.832** (baseline: coverage 0.4405, interval score 3.605).

### What the predictor is
A stateless, stdlib-only (`import math`) linear/ridge predictor, coefficients embedded in the file (no file I/O, no identity features, no absolute clock).

1. **Relative clock only.** The single time-like quantity is `len(history)` (minutes of causal history seen). `time_min` values are never read, so independently shifted clocks change nothing.
2. **Features from causal history only** (all `None`-tolerant, medians as defaults): time-basis (`n/40`, square, `exp(-n/25)`, `sqrt n`), workload level/trend (`watts/mass`, current vs mean, mech work), heart-rate level/trend/drift (last, 3-min mean, max, slope, HR reserve, HR-per-W/kg, HR minus load expectation), skin temperature (last, 3-min mean, min, slope), ambient temperature, humidity, skin−ambient gradient, and anthropometrics (age, mass, height, BMI) — plus load×time, HR×time, HR×mass, HR×ambient interactions.
3. **Target**: core temperature 15 min after the last observed row.
4. **Training-row choice matched to the 3A request distribution**: only origins at/after the first workload decrease were used (this alone moved LOO from ~0.22 to ~0.15); equal weight per person because the metric is person-balanced; corrupted core-temp readings (impossible jumps/`null`s in H04/H07/H09) excluded.

Final answer — frozen predictor and research summary.

## Frozen predictor (submission.py)

A population-trajectory model. From `train.json` (14 labeled people, 60 min sessions each), I computed the per-session-minute **median** core temperature across people, lightly smoothed with a centered 5-minute moving average. For a 3A request, the prediction is `CURVE[origin_minute + 15]`, where the origin minute is computed **relative to the first history row** (`t_last − t_first + 1`), making it robust to the independently shifted clocks in hidden testing; the curve is clamped flat outside minutes 1–60. The 90% interval is fixed and asymmetric: `[mean − 0.95, mean + 0.70]` (width 1.65 ≤ 5 C). The code is stateless, uses only causal history fields, handles 3B requests sensibly (curve at the current minute), and has defensive fallbacks for missing/empty inputs.

## Development evidence (actual dev_score runs)

| model | person-balanced MAE | MAE | coverage90 | interval score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| template baseline | 0.539 | 0.520 | 0.44 | 3.60 |
| raw median curve, ±0.5ish | 0.299 | 0.312 | 0.76 | 2.85 |
| curve + mass adjustment | 0.335 | 0.371 | 0.74 | 3.86 |
| smoothed curve, −0.9/+0.62 | 0.2985 | 0.3114 | 0.94 | 2.20 |
| **final: smoothed curve, −0.95/+0.70** | **0.2985** | **0.3114** | **0.964** | **2.27** |

## Why this model

Leave-one-person-out (LOPO) experiments on the 190 training 3A origins (9 people with a watts decrease) showed that cross-person forecasting is dominated by unobservable person-level offsets (~±0.3–0.8 C): ridge/GBM/random-forest on 32 engineered causal features (HR, skin, watts, trends, cumulative work, anthropometrics, ECTemp-style filter output) all **lost** to a constant (ridge 0.37–0.97, GBM 0.31, RF 0.25, constant 0.225, time-indexed median curve 0.223 LOPO pb-MAE). No single feature transferred across people (best single-feature LOPO ≈ constant), and person-level offset correlations with mass/BSA/%HRmax/skin were weak (|r| ≤ 0.38, n=14). A mass-based offset adjustment helped slightly in LOPO (0.2234→0.2147) but **hurt on dev** (0.299→0.335), so it was reverted — concrete evidence that person-offset corrections do not generalize here. The time curve, in contrast, carries real structure (population core rises ~37.35→38.68 C with deceleration) and transfers: dev hot-subset MAE was 0.086.

## Causal inputs used

Only `time_min` of the first and last history rows (relative elapsed time) and `horizon_min`. All other fields were evaluated and deliberately excluded based on LOPO plus dev evidence.

## Uncertainty and limitations

Interval offsets came from LOPO residual quantiles (5th/95th ≈ −0.46/+0.41) widened for cross-person offsets observed in train (−0.37 to +0.64) and dev (one person ≈ −0.76); dev coverage 0.964, interval score 2.27. Main limitations: (1) between-person core offsets are irreducible with these sensors in this sample — one dev person contributes MAE 0.76 while the other three are 0.10–0.19; (2) the curve assumes hidden sessions follow a similar heat-exercise protocol and that history starts at session start (true in dev); sessions much longer than 60 min would be clamped to the plateau value; (3) n=14 training people limits any richer model — more flexible models consistently overfit in LOPO.

## Frozen predictor

`submission.py` (stateless, pure-stdlib at inference) estimates current core temperature as a **50/50 blend of two ExtraTrees forests**, trained offline on the 14 labeled training people (836 minute-level samples) and exported to JSON (`model_lean.json`, `model_full.json`) that submission.py traverses in pure Python — no sklearn/numpy/pickle needed at predict time:

- **Lean forest** (300 trees, min_samples_leaf=40, 7 features): elapsed-time ramp `min(rel_t,30)`, cumulative HR-above-80 load, the same load mass-normalized, elapsed-time × smoothed(EWMA-15) HR excess, first watts, current watts, BMI.
- **Full forest** (300 trees, leaf=56, 37 features): adds skin temperature level/EWMAs/trends, ambient, humidity, demographics, work integrals, missingness flags — a hedge in case skin/ambient carry signal for unseen people or HR is missing.

Interval: fixed `mean ± 0.65 °C` (width 1.3 ≤ 5), clipped mean to [35.5, 41.0]; safe fallback (37.3 ± 1.0) for empty/broken histories.

## Causal inputs and invariances
Only the provided history is used. All time features are differences from the first history row (verified prediction-identical under a +7777-min clock shift). Missing channels are forward-filled causally, with defaults and missingness indicators; integrals assume the observed 1-min cadence.

## Development evidence (actually run)
- Template baseline: dev person-balanced MAE **0.388**, coverage 0.717, interval score 2.19, score 0.721.

- Dev scores: full-feature ET **0.2618**; lean ET 0.2645 (LOPO selection slightly overfit); frozen blend **0.2618** pbMAE, hot-subset MAE **0.072**, coverage **0.923**, interval score **1.88**, score **0.792**.
- Interval calibrated on LOPO residuals (pooled q05/q95 ≈ −0.45/+0.53); ±0.65 chosen as a robustness buffer (LOPO coverage 0.955; per-time-bucket quantiles checked — asymmetric/adaptive variants offered ≤~0.1 interval-score gain and were rejected as riskier).

I've built `submission.py` for 3A. On dev it scores a person-balanced MAE of 0.282, against 0.539 for the template baseline. But one of the four dev people is badly missed (0.92 C error), and on the training data the model barely beats predicting a constant.

**How it works**
- **Model:** a single linear model, equal to an even average of two median-regression fits, both trained on every forecast origin in `train.json` (14 people). Coefficients are fixed in the file; it imports only `math` and reads no files.
  - Fit 1 uses only time: log(elapsed + 15).
  - Fit 2 adds initial watts per kg, time × initial watts per kg, and BMI.
- **Inputs:** elapsed time is counted from the first history row, so shifted clocks don't change anything (a +500 min shift gave identical output). It also uses initial watts, mass and height. HR, skin, ambient and humidity are not used, because none of them improved leave-one-person-out results.
- **Missing values:** filled with defaults; an all-null or empty history still returns a valid answer.
- **Interval:** prediction −0.6 to +0.6 C (width 1.2).

**Development results** (person-balanced MAE)

| Model | Leave-one-person-out on train (9 people with scored origins) | Dev (4 people) |
|---|---|---|
| Template baseline | — | 0.539 (coverage 0.44, interval score 3.60) |
| Covariate fit alone (least squares) | 0.212 | 0.343 |
| Time only | 0.263 | 0.270 |
| **Final average** | **0.226** | **0.282** |

- **Per dev person (final):** H08 0.067, H17 0.917, H20 0.015, H24 0.128. Interval coverage was 0.75 and interval score 3.45.
- **Why I chose the average:** across all 13 people it comes out around 0.243, versus about 0.252 for the covariate fit and 0.265 for time only. Those gaps are within noise.
- **Interval tuning used dev:** the leave-one-person-out residual quantiles (about −0.32/+0.52) gave dev coverage of only about 0.74. I widened the interval to ±0.6 partly because of H17's dev miss. That brought the dev interval score from 4.54 to 3.45, with no change to the point predictions.

**Limitations**
- **Person offset dominates:** each person's own core-temperature level is the main source of error, and it can't be seen in the inputs. A constant prediction already gets 0.238 on the training check, so the covariates add little.
- **Training pattern can fail:** in training, people on lower watts started with higher core temps. Dev person H17 (low watts) broke that pattern and the model over-predicted by about 0.9 C. The template's HR/skin estimate happened to fit H17 well but missed the other three people badly. People like H17 will likely be missed again and fall outside the interval.
- **Small evidence base:** 9 scored training people and 4 dev people, and I used dev to choose between candidates. The reported numbers are therefore optimistic.
- **Clock-shift assumption:** I assumed each history begins at the start of the session, as all dev requests do.

I also tried an HR-based Kalman-filter estimate, HR drift, skin drift, alternative time curves and least-squares versions. None was a reliable improvement, so none is in the final model.

I've built and frozen `submission.py`. On the 5 development people its person-balanced MAE is **0.208 °C**, down from 0.388 °C for the template. The file is self-contained, uses only the Python standard library (`math`), and has the coefficients written into it.

**How it works**
1. **Main model (ridge regression).** Fitted on all 14 training people (840 labelled minutes). It uses three inputs:
   - elapsed time, as `1 − exp(−elapsed/60)`;
   - current watts, carried forward over gaps;
   - the product of the two.

   Elapsed time is counted from the history's first `time_min`, falling back to the row count if the clock looks inconsistent. The fit is roughly: core ≈ 38.24 − 0.00508·W + (1.03 + 0.0080·W)·(1 − e^(−t/60)). In the training data, people on higher workloads started cooler but heated up faster, and everyone ended near 38.9 °C at 60 min.
2. **Heart-rate correction.** The final estimate is 0.8 × the ridge estimate + 0.2 × the output of an ECTemp-style Kalman filter. The filter uses only heart rate, with standard parameters from the published literature (start at 37.1 °C, step noise 0.022, the usual heart-rate-to-temperature curve). I didn't tune them on these data.
   - The correction is capped at ±0.6 °C.
   - It is switched off if no valid heart rate (30–230 bpm) has appeared after minute 8.
3. **3A requests.** The ridge model is evaluated at elapsed time + `horizon_min` (15), plus the same heart-rate correction. 3A wasn't scored here, so this path is untested.

Every input comes from the causal history only. Nothing depends on the absolute clock or on who the person is. I checked that shifting the clock by 537 minutes gives identical output. All-null rows and histories with no heart rate still return valid, finite results.

**90% interval.** The lower and upper offsets are the 5th and 95th percentiles of leave-one-person-out errors, in four elapsed-time bands (≤10, ≤25, ≤40, >40 min). They are widened by 1.2 to allow for new people, with each side kept within 2.4 °C. On dev the intervals are 1.0–1.7 °C wide.

**Results**

| Version | Leave-one-person-out MAE (train) | Dev MAE | Dev 90% coverage | Dev interval score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Template | 0.53 (scored on its own) | 0.388 | 0.72 | 2.19 |
| Ridge only | 0.243 | 0.269 | 0.83 | 1.89 |
| Ridge + age (median regression) | 0.204 | 0.323 | 0.73 | 2.44 |
| **Final: ridge + 0.2 heart-rate filter** | **0.244** | **0.208** | **0.917** | **1.856** |

- **What I rejected.** None of these beat ridge-only in leave-one-person-out testing: heart rate and skin temperature as direct inputs, cumulative work per kg, mass, BMI, height, humidity, gradient boosting and random forests.
- **Age.** Adding age looked better on training people but was clearly worse on dev, so I dropped it.
- **The heart-rate weight.** A weight of 0.1–0.2 made no difference on training people, so I tested 0.2 once on dev. I didn't search for the best dev weight.
- **Start value.** Starting the filter at 37.3 °C fit the training people slightly better, but I kept the literature default of 37.1 °C rather than tune it to this cohort.

On dev, per-person MAE is 0.06–0.09 °C for three people but 0.47 (H17) and 0.34 (H21) for the other two. Requests flagged as hot (61 of 300) have MAE 0.04.

**Limitations**
- **Small sample.** There are only 14 training people and 5 dev people, so differences of about 0.01–0.03 °C are within noise.
- **Dev influenced one choice.** I used the dev score to decide to keep the heart-rate correction and drop age, so the 0.208 is somewhat optimistic.
- **Starting temperature is the main error.** Each person's starting core temperature is only partly predictable from workload, and most of the remaining error is a constant offset per person.
- **Cohort level.** Dev people seem to run cooler than training people. If test people differ again, the overall level could be off.
- **Missing heart rate.** Without heart rate the model falls back to time and workload alone, which was 0.27 on dev.
- **Unusual workloads.** Very low or zero watts, or sessions much longer than 60 minutes, are outside the training range.

The helper files `feats.py`, `kf.py`, `cv.py`, `gen.py` and `sub_ridge_B.py` are also in the workspace, but `submission.py` doesn't need them.
